1.pericope_label: And God remembered Noah, and made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged

schools.summary: Gill reads the remembering as an accommodation to Noah's own experience. God does not, and cannot, properly speaking, forget his creatures; but this is said after the manner of men, and as it might have seemed to Noah, who, having heard nothing from God for five months, and having been perhaps longer in the ark than he expected, might begin to think that he was forgotten. God remembered him, and his covenant with him, and the promise he had made him that he and his family and all the living creatures should be preserved alive during the flood — and he may be said particularly to remember them when he began to take measures for removing the waters from the earth. Gill adds the general rule the phrase carries, that God's helping his people when in distress, and delivering them out of it, is called his remembrance of them. On the stopping of the fountains he passes on Jarchi's observation, that it is not said that all the fountains of the deep were stopped, as it was said that all were broken up, because some were left open for the use and benefit of the world, and because some must be left for the waters to return into. Calvin insists that the word be referred not only to the external aspect of things but to the inward feeling of the holy man. It is certain that God, from the time he had once received Noah into his protection, was never unmindful of him, for it was by as great a miracle that he did not perish through suffocation in the ark as if he had lived without breath, submerged in the waters. But as the ark was floating even to the fifth month, the delay by which the Lord suffered his servant to be anxiously and miserably tortured might seem to imply a kind of oblivion; and Calvin does not question that Noah's heart was agitated by various feelings when he found himself so long held in suspense, for he might infer that his life had been prolonged in order that he might be more miserable than any of the rest of mankind — since we are accustomed to imagine God absent except when we have some sensible experience of his presence. On the chronology Calvin distinguishes between two reckonings. Some include the forty days of continued rain in the whole period, but he holds that until the fortieth day the waters rose gradually by fresh additions, and then remained nearly in the same state for a hundred and fifty days, both computations making the period a little more than six months and a half; while if the seventh month be numbered from the beginning of the year rather than from Noah's entering the ark, the subsidence took place as soon as the ark had floated five months. And he draws a purpose from the length of it: by so lengthened a space of time the Lord would show the more plainly that the dreadful desolation of the world had not fallen upon it accidentally, but was a remarkable proof of his judgment, while the deliverance of Noah was a magnificent work of his grace, and worthy of everlasting remembrance.

Henry calls the verse an act of God's grace and reads it against the emptied world. The whole race of mankind, except Noah and his family, was now extinguished and driven into the land of forgetfulness, to be remembered no more, so that God's remembering Noah was the return of his mercy to mankind, of whom he would not make a full end. The demands of divine justice had been answered by the ruin of those sinners; he had eased himself of his adversaries, and now his spirit was quieted — he remembered mercy in wrath, remembered the days of old, remembered the holy seed, and then remembered Noah. Henry adds that Noah himself, though one who had found grace in the eyes of the Lord, seemed to be forgotten in the ark, and perhaps began to think himself so, since we do not find that God had told him how long his confinement should last or when he should be released; and he observes that very good men have sometimes been ready to draw the same conclusion about themselves.

Clarke takes the wind for such a wind as produced a strong and sudden evaporation, and reports that the effects of these winds, which are frequent in the east, are truly astonishing. He instances the account of a friend who, having been bathing in the Tigris not far from the ancient city of Ctesiphon and within five days' journey of Bagdad, was caught by one of the hot winds which the natives call samiel as it passed rapidly across. Wesley states the remembering in the same terms Henry uses, that it is an expression after the manner of men, since not any of God's creatures, much less any of his people, are forgotten of him: the whole race of mankind except Noah and his family was now extinguished and gone into the land of forgetfulness, so that God's remembering Noah was the return of his mercy to mankind. Noah himself, though one that had found grace in the eyes of the Lord, seemed to be forgotten in the ark, but at length God returned in mercy to him, and that is expressed by his remembering him. On the ebb Wesley notes the Hebrew idiom, that the waters were going and returning, a gradual departure, the heat of the sun exhaling much and the subterraneous caverns perhaps soaking in more.

Ellicott attends to the verbs. The waters, he renders, became still; and it is plain from this that the strength of the waters described at the close of the previous chapter has reference to the violent currents, which still existed up to the end of the hundred and fiftieth day, after which they ceased. The wind, which he compares with the creative wind moving over the face of the waters at the beginning, began to blow as soon as the rains ceased, or even before, as must necessarily have been the case with so vast a disturbance of the atmosphere; but its special purpose of assuaging the waters only began when the downpour was over. Ellicott adds the practical observation that this wind would affect the course of the ark, but scarcely so strongly as the currents of the water. On the returning of the waters he sees a further indication that a vast wave from the sea had swept over the land, in addition to the forty days of rain; and he notes what those in the ark would have perceived, that they would notice the changing current and would know by their being aground that the flood was diminishing — the slow abatement and the stillness together making it probable that the ark had grounded on some land-locked spot. He also observes on the divine name that Elohim stands here where, on the Jehovistic theory, one would have expected Jehovah.

4.pericope_label: And the ark rested upon the mountains of Ararat; and the tops of the mountains were seen

schools.summary: Gill works out the date and reports the rival reckonings. The resting was five months after the flood began, and this is not the seventh month of the flood but of the year, which, being reckoned from Tisri or the autumnal equinox, must be the month Nisan, answering to part of March and part of April — as the Targum of Jonathan explains it, saying that this is the month Nisan. But Jarchi makes it the month Sivan, answering to part of May and part of June, taking it to be the seventh month from Cisleu, when the forty days' rain ceased; and Dr. Lightfoot follows him in that. According to Bishop Usher, Gill adds, the seventeenth day of the seventh month on which the ark rested was Wednesday the sixth of May. On the following verse he measures the interval, from the seventeenth of the seventh month to the first of the tenth, a space of two months and thirteen days, and notes that it was summer time, so that through the heat of the sun the waters decreased apace.

Clarke takes up the site of the resting and clears away a legend. That Ararat was a mountain of Armenia is almost universally agreed, and what is commonly thought to be the Ararat of the Scriptures has been visited by many travellers, and there are several monasteries on it. For a long time, he says, the world has been amused with reports that the remains of the ark were still visible there, but Tournefort, a famous French naturalist who was on the spot, assures us that nothing of the kind is to be seen. Since there is a great chain of mountains called by this name it is impossible to determine on what part of them the ark rested, though the highest part, called by some the finger mountain, has been fixed on as the most likely place — and these things, Clarke judges, are certainly of very little consequence. From the circumstance of the resting on the seventeenth day of the seventh month he passes on a curious conclusion of Dr. Lightfoot's, that the ark drew exactly eleven cubits of water, since on the first day of the month Ab the mountain tops were first seen, by which time the waters had fallen fifteen cubits. Wesley states the same calculation from the other end, that they felt ground above forty days before they saw it, whence Lightfoot infers, if the waters decreased proportionably, that the ark drew eleven cubits; and on the resting itself he agrees that the ark was directed to the mountains of Ararat, or Armenia, not by Noah's prudence but by the wise providence of God.

Ellicott confirms the arithmetic from the calendar and then questions the geography. Since the months had each thirty days, the interval makes exactly a hundred and fifty days from the beginning of the flood; and taking the seventh civil month for Abib, he passes on a set of coincidences noticed in the Speaker's Commentary — that on the seventeenth day of Abib the ark rested on Mount Ararat, on the seventeenth day of Abib the Israelites passed over the Red Sea, and on the seventeenth day of Abib Christ our Lord rose again from the dead. On the mountains themselves he doubts the Armenian identification. If the Authorised Version is right in saying that the descendants of Noah travelled from the east to Shinar, this could not be the Ararat of Armenia; the word in Assyrian means highland, and thus may signify any hilly country; and in the Chaldean Genesis the ark rests upon Nizir, a region to the east of Assyria, the highest peak of which, now named Elwend, is called in the cuneiform texts the mountain of the world. Ellicott concedes that the rendering from the east is by no means certain, many translating eastward instead.

Henry treats the resting and the appearing of the mountain tops as the effects and evidences of the ebbing of the waters, and draws the comfort out of each. It was some satisfaction to Noah to feel the house he was in upon firm ground, and no longer movable; and it rested upon a mountain whither it was directed, not by Noah's prudence, for he did not steer it, but by the wise and gracious providence of God, that it might rest the sooner. From this Henry takes his note, that God has times and places of rest for his people after their tossings, and that many a time he provides for their seasonable and comfortable settlement without their own contrivance and quite beyond their own foresight — the ark of the church, though sometimes tossed with tempests and not comforted, having nevertheless its rests. Of the mountain tops he observes that they appeared like little islands above the water, and that we must suppose they were seen by Noah and his sons, for there were none besides to see them; it is probable, he adds, that they had looked through the window of the ark every day, like longing mariners after a tedious voyage, to see whether they could discover land.

6.pericope_label: Noah opened the window and sent forth a raven, and afterward the dove, which returned unto him

schools.summary: Clarke sets himself against the common reading of the raven's flight. It is generally supposed that the raven flew off and was seen no more, but this meaning the Hebrew text will not bear, since the words say that it went forth, going forth and returning — from which it is evident that she did return, though she was not taken into the ark. She made frequent excursions, and continued on the wing as long as she could, having picked up such aliment as she found floating on the waters, and then, to rest herself, regained the ark, where she might perch though she was not admitted. Indeed this must be allowed, Clarke argues, as it is impossible she could have continued twenty-one days upon the wing, which she must have done had she not returned; and the text itself is sufficiently determinate. On the dove he traces the three sendings: the first time she speedily returned, having in all probability gone but a little way from the ark, as she must naturally be terrified at the appearance of the waters; after seven days, being sent out a second time, she returned with an olive leaf plucked off, an emblem of the restoration of peace between God and the earth, from which circumstance the olive has been the emblem of peace among all civilized nations; and at the end of the other seven days, being sent out the third time, she returned no more, from which Noah conjectured that the earth was now sufficiently drained and therefore removed the covering of the ark. Wesley reads the raven's flight the same way, that it went forth going forth and returning, that is, flying about but returning to the ark for rest, probably not in it but upon it — which gave Noah little satisfaction. Of the dove he says she returned the first time with no good news, but probably wet and dirty, while the second time she brought an olive leaf in her bill which appeared to be freshly plucked off, a plain indication that the trees were now beginning to appear above water. Wesley notes the regularity of the intervals, that Noah sent the dove the second time seven days after the first, and the third after seven days too, and that probably the first sending of her was seven days after the sending forth of the raven.

Calvin uses the forty days' delay as a window into Noah's state of mind. We may hence conjecture, he says, with what great anxiety the breast of the holy man was oppressed: after he had perceived the ark to be resting on solid ground, he yet did not dare to open the window till the fortieth day — not because he was stunned and torpid, but because an example thus formidable of the vengeance of God had affected him with such fear and sorrow combined that, being deprived of all judgment, he silently remained in the chamber of his ark. On the raven Calvin explains the choice of bird: he has no doubt that Noah purposely selected the raven, which he knew might be allured by the odour of carcasses to take a further flight, if the earth with the animals upon it were already exposed to view; but the raven, perceiving nothing but muddy marshes, hovers around and immediately seeks to be readmitted. Gill gives the same reason for the choice — the raven is a bird of prey which feeds on carrion, so that if the earth had been dry the smell of the dead carcasses would have invited it to go far from the ark and not return, whereas if not, Noah would see it again. On the dove Gill explains why her failure was the more telling: she is a creature that feeds upon seeds picked off the ground and loves cleanness, and so could find no place where she could alight and have food and yet retain her cleanness, for though the tops of the mountains were clear of the waters they might be muddy and filthy with what the waters had raised up in them or left upon them; and therefore she returned to Noah again, and not only like the raven unto the ark, but into it. Of her evening return he notes that she had been out all day delighting herself in a free air and perching upon the trees, but not finding sufficient food or a proper lodging, came back at evening for food and dwelling in the ark; and he dates the opening of the window to the eleventh day of the eleventh month, the month Ab, which Usher fixed as Friday the twenty-eighth of August.

Henry asks why Noah, who had been told the flood's coming to a day, was left to discover its departure for himself, and answers from the difference between the two kinds of knowledge. The knowledge of the former was necessary to his preparing the ark and settling himself in it, but the knowledge of the latter would have served only to gratify his curiosity, and the concealing of it from him was the needful exercise of his faith and patience; and while he could not foresee the flood except by revelation, he might by ordinary means discover its decrease, and therefore God was pleased to leave him to the use of them. Henry treats the two birds as the spies Noah sent forth to bring him intelligence from abroad, and observes that though Noah by faith expected his enlargement, and by patience waited for it, he was not without concern to know when it should come.

Keil and Delitzsch note that the Hebrew says the raven, that is, the particular raven known from that circumstance, and that Noah let it fly out for the purpose of ascertaining the drying up of the waters. It went out and returned until the earth was dry, but without being taken back into the ark, since the mountain tops and the carcases floating upon the water afforded it both a resting place and food. Ellicott identifies the window as not the zohar named in the account of the ark's building but an aperture, and explains the choice of the raven: it was chosen as one strong of flight, perhaps also because anciently regarded as prophetic of the weather, and because it is easily tamed — and since Noah retained its mate, he had security for its return, so that each night it returned to the ark, and probably to its old perch near the female. He reports the rival tradition without adopting it, that the Chaldean Genesis agrees with many commentators and with the ancient versions in supposing that the raven did not return, having found abundant food in the floating dead bodies. On the timing he observes that Noah had waited forty days after seeing the heights around him rising clearly into the air, and then, impatient of the slow subsidence of the waters, sent the bird out to bring him some news of the state of the earth.

13.pericope_label: Noah removed the covering of the ark, and the face of the ground was dry; and the earth was dried

schools.summary: Henry distinguishes the two stages the passage marks, the ground dry and the ground dried. All the water was carried off it, which upon the first day of the first month — a joyful new year's day it was — Noah was himself an eye-witness of. He removed the covering of the ark, not the whole covering, but so much as would suffice to give him a prospect of the earth about it, and a most comfortable prospect he had, for behold, behold and wonder, the face of the ground was dry. Henry draws two notes from it. It is a great mercy to see ground about us, and Noah was more sensible of that than we are, since mercies restored are much more affecting than mercies continued. And the divine power which now renewed the face of the earth can renew the face of an afflicted troubled soul, and of a distressed persecuted church, making dry ground appear even where it seemed to have been lost and forgotten. On the second stage he observes that the ground was dried so as to be a fit habitation for Noah, and that though Noah saw the ground dry on the first day of the first month, God kept him waiting nearly two months more before it was fit to live on.

Ellicott sets the whole sequence out as a table and draws two conclusions from it. Reckoning the flood's commencement in the second month, called Marchesvan, on the seventeenth day; the hundred and fifty days during which the waters prevailed, bringing the account to the seventeenth day of the seventh month; the seventy-three days more before the mountain tops were seen on the first day of the tenth month; the forty days before the raven was sent; and the three sendings of the dove at intervals of seven days — he finds that the day named here falls exactly one month after the dove was last let go. What strikes him is the pace: it was thus very slowly that the earth returned to its normal state. His second inference is drawn from the sevens rather than the totals, since the intervals of seven days between the sending forth of the birds prove that the division of time into weeks was fully established, and suggest besides that religious observances were connected with it. On the later verse Ellicott dates it fifty-seven days after Noah removed the covering, and a year and eleven days after the flood began, and notes that the word rendered dried there is different from the words translated dried up and dry in the earlier verse, marking a further stage in the process, so that it should be translated was thoroughly dry. He also offers an explanation of the calendar: it is reasonably certain that thirty days were reckoned to a month, but twelve lunar months make not three hundred and sixty days but only about three hundred and fifty-four, so that probably the day of the new moon was often twice counted, as the last of the old month and the first of the new — and if to those days the eleven from the seventeenth to the twenty-seventh be added, the result is exactly a full solar year.

Clarke computes the time in the ark and finds it a complete solar year. Noah entered on the seventeenth day of the second month in the six hundredth year of his life, and continued until the twenty-seventh day of the second month in the six hundred and first; the months of the ancient Hebrews were lunar, the first six consisting of thirty days each and the latter six of twenty-nine, so that the whole twelve made three hundred and fifty-four days. Add to this the eleven days between the seventeenth and the twenty-seventh, and the total is exactly three hundred and sixty-five days, the period of a complete solar revolution — the odd hours and minutes, as being fractions of time, not computed. Wesley records the same two moments briefly, that Noah removed not the whole covering but so much as would suffice to give him a prospect of the earth about it, and that the earth was dried so as to be a fit habitation for him.

Gill reaches the same solar year as Clarke by the same arithmetic, and then doubts the premise it rests on. He notes that Noah went into the ark on the seventeenth of this month, so that he was in it twelve months and ten days according to a solar year, and that if the reckoning be made according to Jewish months, six of thirty days and six of twenty-nine only, the twelve months make three hundred and fifty-four days, to which eleven days added make three hundred and sixty-five — so that Noah was in the ark just a full year according to the course of the sun. Yet it seems very plain to Gill that the months reckoned here consisted of thirty days apiece, since the hundred and fifty days during which the waters prevailed are counted from the seventeenth day of one month to the seventeenth of another. He identifies the month as Marchesvan, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, answering to part of October and part of November, and records that according to Bishop Usher the day was Friday the eighteenth of December; and he notes that the Septuagint adds the words in the first month to the opening notice of the six hundred and first year.

15.pericope_label: And God spake unto Noah, saying, Go forth of the ark; and Noah went forth, and every living thing

schools.summary: Henry fastens on the one fact that governs the section, that Noah did not stir till God bade him. As he had a command to go into the ark, so, however tedious his confinement there had been, he would wait for a command to go out of it again. From this Henry draws his rule: we must in all our ways acknowledge God, and set him before us in all our removes, since those only go under God's protection who follow God's direction and submit to his government. Those who steadily adhere to God's word as their rule, who are guided by his grace as their principle, and who take hints from his providence to assist them in applying general directions to particular cases, may in faith see him guiding their motions in their march through this wilderness. And Henry adds the consolation that answers the delay — though God detained him long, at last he gave him his discharge, for the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak, and shall speak truth, and shall not lie. He also notices the change in the wording of the two commands, that God had said, Come into the ark, and now says, Go forth of it.

Calvin praises the same restraint and anticipates the objection to it. Though Noah was not a little terrified at the judgment of God, his patience is commended in this respect, that having the earth before his eyes, which offered him a home, he yet does not venture to go forth. Profane men may ascribe such waiting to timidity, or even to indolence; but holy is that timidity which is produced by the obedience of faith, and Noah was restrained by a hallowed modesty from allowing himself to enjoy the bounty of nature until he should hear the voice of God directing him to do so. Moses winds the matter up in a few words, Calvin says, but the thing itself deserves attention: all ought spontaneously to consider how great must have been the fortitude of a man who, after the incredible weariness of a whole year, when the deluge has ceased and new life has shone forth, does not yet move a foot out of his sepulchre without the command of God — so that by a continual course of faith the holy man was obedient to God. Of the command to bring out the creatures Calvin hears a word of comfort, since with these words the Lord would cheer the mind of Noah and inspire him with confidence that a seed had been preserved in the ark which should increase till it replenished the whole earth. The renovation of the earth is promised to Noah, to the end that he may know that the world itself was enclosed in the ark, and that the solitude and devastation at the sight of which his heart might faint would not be perpetual. Gill fills in the manner of the command and of the obedience. Whether God spoke in a dream or vision, or by an articulate voice appearing in human form, or by an impulse on the mind, is not certain, but the Lord spoke so that Noah heard and understood him; and it was no doubt very rejoicing to Noah, since he had not heard that voice for a year or more, at least that we read of. Though the earth was dry and fit to be inhabited, Gill notes, Noah would not go out without orders, as he had gone in with them, and waited for them until now he has them. On the command to bring forth the creatures he records a various reading: according to the margin, as Jarchi observes, the sense is to order them to come forth, and according to the Scripture, if they will not, to oblige them to come. And Noah went forth being obedient to the divine command, no doubt with great pleasure in his countenance and with a heart full of thankfulness for so great a deliverance — all the creatures going out with him, and not one left behind.

20.pericope_label: And Noah builded an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings on the altar

schools.summary: Henry notices that this is the first thing Noah does without being told. Hitherto he had done nothing without particular instructions and commands from God, having had a particular call into the ark and another out of it; but altars and sacrifices being already of divine institution for religious worship, he did not stay for a particular command in order to express his thankfulness. Those who have received mercy from God should be forward in returning thanks, and should do it not of constraint but willingly, for God is pleased with free-will offerings and with praises that wait for him. Henry then sets the act against the circumstances: Noah was now turned out into a cold and desolate world, where one would have thought his first care would have been to build a house for himself, and behold, he begins with an altar for God — for God, who is the first, must be first served, and he begins well who begins with God. On the sacrifice itself he observes that Noah offered only those beasts and fowls that were clean, since it is not enough that we sacrifice, but we must sacrifice what God appoints, according to the law of sacrifice and not a corrupt thing; and that though his stock of cattle was so small, and had been rescued from ruin at so great an expense of care and pains, he did not grudge what was to be offered.

Clarke makes this altar a hinge of the whole history. Adam, Cain and Abel had offered sacrifices, and there can be no doubt that they had altars on which they offered them, but this one built by Noah is certainly the first on record; and it is worthy of remark that as the old world began with sacrifice, so also did the new. Religion, or the proper mode of worshipping the Divine Being, is the invention or institution of God himself, and sacrifice, in the act and in the design, is the essence of religion — without sacrifice, actually offered or implied, there never was, and there never can be, any religion, even in heaven a lamb being represented before the throne of God as newly slain. The design of sacrificing Clarke takes to be twofold: the slaying and burning of the victim point out, first, that the life of the sinner is forfeited to divine justice, and second, that his soul deserves the fire of perdition. He reports without deciding the Jewish tradition that the place where Noah built his altar was the same in which stood the altar built by Adam and used by Cain and Abel, and the same spot on which Abraham afterwards offered up his son Isaac; and he notes that the Hebrew word we render altar signifies properly a place for sacrifice, the root signifying simply to slay, while our own word comes from the Latin for high, because places for sacrifice were generally raised. Wesley states the point Henry makes about the absence of a command, that hitherto Noah had done nothing without particular instructions from God, but altars and sacrifices being already of divine institution he did not stay for a particular command thus to express his thankfulness; and he identifies the victims as one of every clean beast and fowl, the odd seventh that the earlier chapter had provided.

Gill sets the altar against the house Noah did not build: he raised not a house for himself and his family but an altar for God, his first and greatest concern being for the glory of God and not for the temporal good of himself and his. The altar was erected and devoted to the service of God, built according to his will and by his direction, and Noah's view in it was to renew the worship of God and to preserve and propagate it by his example; the act was a thanksgiving for his wonderful preservation, and was also propitiatory and typical of Christ. Gill then reports and rejects the tradition Clarke leaves standing: the Jewish writers say this was the altar on which Adam sacrificed when expelled from the garden of Eden, and on which Cain and Abel offered, and that being demolished by the flood it was rebuilt by Noah — which Gill judges not at all probable. It is much more likely, he says with Aben Ezra, that it was built on one of the mountains of Ararat, and that as Noah took the first opportunity, so he built it in the first place he came to, or at least not far from the place where he came out of the ark. Calvin reads the sacrifice as an example of gratitude following many proofs of obedience, and takes the passage to teach that sacrifices were instituted from the beginning to this end, that men should habituate themselves by such exercises to celebrate the goodness of God and to give him thanks. The bare confession of the tongue, he grants, or even the silent acknowledgment of the heart, might suffice for God, but we know how many stimulants our indolence requires, so that when the holy fathers formerly professed their piety by sacrifices the use of them was by no means superfluous. Besides, it was right that they should always have before their eyes symbols by which they would be admonished that they could have no access to God but through a mediator — though now the manifestation of Christ has taken away these ancient shadows, and we are to use the helps the Lord has prescribed instead.

Ellicott turns the verse against a critical theory. The account of this sacrificial act is said to have been an interpolation of the Jehovist, but it really forms an integral portion of the numerous traditions of the flood — for in the Chaldean Genesis, after the sending forth of a dove, a swallow and a raven, the survivor says that he sent them forth to the four winds, sacrificed a sacrifice, and built an altar on the peak of the mountain. This extreme antiquity of sections ascribed to the Jehovist, and supposed to be an after-thought, Ellicott judges seriously detrimental to the whole theory. He then explains why an altar was needed at all. One result of the flood was to sweep away all traces of the earthly paradise and of the subsequent abode of Adam, and it is probable also that Noah was removed far away from his previous home by the floating of the ark, so that to him and his family it was a new earth, with no holy places and no spots hallowed by the past history of man. He therefore determines to consecrate the earth to Jehovah, who had been the object of the worship of his family since the days of Enos, and builds an altar, the first mentioned in the Bible — by so doing providing for future generations a central spot and sanctuary round which their religious ideas would group themselves. Ellicott adds that the animals offered were probably the seventh of all clean kinds.

21.pericope_label: And the LORD smelled a sweet savour, and said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground

schools.summary: Calvin will not let the sweet savour be taken literally. Moses calls that by which God was appeased an odour of rest, as if he had said that the sacrifice had been rightly offered; yet nothing can be more absurd than to suppose that God should have been appeased by the filthy smoke of entrails and of flesh. Moses here, according to his manner, invests God with a human character for the purpose of accommodating himself to the capacity of an ignorant people; for it is not even to be supposed that the rite of sacrifice was in itself grateful to God as a meritorious act, but we must regard the end of the work and not confine ourselves to the external form. What else, Calvin asks, did Noah propose to himself than to acknowledge that he had received his own life, and the life of the animals, as the gift of God's mercy alone? That piety breathed a good and sweet odour before God, as the psalmist says when he asks what he shall render unto the Lord for all his benefits. On the promise Calvin notes the weight of the expression that God said it in his heart: although God never retracts what he has openly spoken with his mouth, we are more deeply affected when we hear that he has fixed upon something in his own mind, because an inward decree of this kind in no way depends upon creatures. Gill takes the savour as a savour of rest, with which God was delighted and well pleased, the sacrifice being offered up in the faith of the sacrifice of Christ — the apostle's phrase about a sweet-smelling savour referring, he says, to this passage — since that sacrifice was a satisfaction to the justice of God, an appeasing of his wrath, and a propitiation for the sins of men.

Clarke reads the savour as God being well pleased with a religious act performed in obedience to his own appointment and in faith of the promised Saviour, and finds the type confirmed by Paul, whose words about an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour are the very words used by the Septuagint in this place. On the promise he presses two points of grammar. The verb means I will not add to curse the ground, that is, there shall not be another deluge to destroy the whole earth; and the clause about man's heart he reads concessively — although the imagination of man's heart should be evil, that is, should men become afterwards as evil as they have been before, God will not destroy the earth by a flood. Clarke then adds the qualification which keeps the promise from being a reprieve from judgment altogether: God has other means of destruction, and the next time he visits by a general judgment, fire is to be the agent. Wesley glosses the savour as a savour of rest, God being well pleased with Noah's pious zeal and these hopeful beginnings of the new world, as men are with fragrant and agreeable smells. On the promise he traces the history of the curse: God had cursed the ground upon the first entrance of sin, and when he drowned it he added to that curse, but now he determines not to add to it any more — meaning that whatever ruin God might bring upon particular persons, families or countries, he would never again destroy the whole world till the day when time shall be no more. Wesley then confronts the reason given, which he calls surprising, since it seems the same as the reason given for the destruction of the world. But there is this difference: there it is said that the imagination of man's heart is evil continually, that is, his actual transgressions continually cry against him, while here it is said to be evil from his youth or childhood, so that he brought it into the world with him and was shapen and conceived in it. One would think it should follow that the guilty race be wholly extinguished; instead the conclusion drawn is that God will no more take this severe method, since man is rather to be pitied, and such conduct is but what might be expected from so degenerate a race.

Ellicott renders the Hebrew a smell of satisfaction, and states the sense carefully: the idea is not so much that the sacrifice gave God pleasure as that it caused him to regard man with complacency, the anger at sin which had caused the flood being now over, and there being peace between heaven and earth. The phrase said in his heart is in the Hebrew to his heart, meaning that Jehovah determined with himself and came to a settled purpose. On the reason given for the promise Ellicott meets the critical charge directly. There seems at first sight to be an inconsistency between this passage and the earlier one, and the Jehovist is accused of contradicting the Elohist, since in the former place man's inborn sinfulness is described as an aggravation of his offence while here it is used as a reason for mercy. His answer is that it is a characteristic of the Bible that it states the two sides of every principle with abrupt simplicity, and that most heresies have arisen from seizing upon one side only and omitting the other from view. Man is one whose every imagination of the heart is only evil continually; in the antediluvian world, with death indefinitely postponed, these imaginations had been unrestrained and had therefore led to habitual and inveterate sin, so that justice at last had smitten it. But when man strives against them, and sin is the result of infirmity, then mercy heals and grace strengthens the penitent — and when man began his renewed life by hallowing it with religion, God saw therein the pledge of a struggle.

22.pericope_label: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, shall not cease

schools.summary: Clarke finds something very expressive in the original, which reads until all the days of the earth: God does not reckon its duration by centuries, and the words themselves afford a strong presumption that the earth shall not have an endless duration. On the seasons he stands against the other witnesses. Most European nations divide the year into four distinct parts, called quarters or seasons, but there are six divisions in the text, and probably all are intended to describe the seasons in one of these postdiluvian years, particularly in that part of the globe, Armenia, where Noah was when God gave him, and mankind through him, this gracious promise. He supports the reading from the calendars he can consult: from the Targum of Jonathan on this verse we learn that in Palestine the seed time was in September at the autumnal equinox, the harvest in March at the vernal equinox, the winter beginning in December at the solstice and the summer at the solstice in June, while the Copts begin their autumn on the fifteenth of September and extend it to the fifteenth of December, their winter thence to the fifteenth of March, and so on through the year. He grants that it is difficult to ascertain the seasons here named, but thinks it very probable that those distinctly marked immediately after the deluge are the ones mentioned in this place.

Ellicott rejects the six-season reading and refutes it from the agriculture. The traditional interpretation of this verse among the Jews represents the year as divided into six seasons, but this is untenable, for in Palestine itself there are two seed times, the winter crops being put into the ground in October and November and the summer crops in January and February. Really, he says, the verse describes those great alternations upon which the well-being of the earth depends — whether considered absolutely, as of light and darkness, cold and heat; or with reference to man's labours, as of sowing and harvesting; or relatively with respect to vegetation, winter being the earth's time of rest and summer that of its activity. As regards the promises themselves Ellicott records Delitzsch's view, that they probably came to Noah as strong inward convictions in answer to his prayers during the sacrifice.

Calvin reads the verse as the completion of the world's restoration. By these words the world is again completely restored, for so great was the confusion and disorder which had overspread the earth that there was a necessity for some renovation — on which account Peter speaks of the old world as having perished in the deluge. The deluge, Calvin observes, had been an interruption of the order of nature itself, for the revolutions of the sun and moon had ceased and there was no distinction of winter and summer; and the Lord here declares it to be his pleasure that all things should recover their vigour and be restored to their functions. On the number of the seasons he agrees with Ellicott against Clarke, holding that the Jews erroneously divide their year into six parts, whereas Moses, by placing the summer in opposition to the winter, divides the whole year in a popular manner into two — by cold and heat designating the same periods, and by seed-time and harvest marking those advantages which flow to men from the moderated temperature of the atmosphere. Calvin then meets the objection that this equable temperament is not perceived every year: the answer is ready, that the order of the world is indeed disturbed by our vices, so that many of its movements are irregular, the sun often withholding its proper heat, snow or hail following in the place of dew, and the air agitated by various tempests. Gill hears in the opening clause a limit rather than a guarantee, since the earth as to its substance may remain for ever, yet as to its form and quality will be changed, and it and all in it will be burnt up — the original reading as yet all the days of the earth, which shows that there is a time fixed for its continuance, and that this time is but short, being measured by days. On the seasons he explains what the promise answers to: they had ceased, or seemed to cease, during the flood, for the year past there had been no seedtime nor harvest, and it must have been for the most part damp and cold through the rains and the abundance of water on the earth, so that the difference of the seasons was not very discernible — nor that of day and night at some times, especially when the clouds were so black and thick over the heavens that neither sun, moon nor stars could be seen.
